briefs.name: First Christian Church
briefs.headline: The church that helped Columbus see modern architecture differently
facts: Eliel Saarinen designed the church, completed in 1942. Its restrained geometry uses buff brick and limestone, a prominent facade cross and a separate campanile.
https://visitcolumbusindiana.com/directory/first-christian-church/
The visitor center identifies it as the city’s first contemporary building. Treat that as the local source’s historical characterization rather than an uncited global superlative.

briefs.name: The LEX / former North Christian Church
briefs.headline: From sanctuary to shared space: the next life of North Christian
facts: Eero Saarinen’s church was completed in 1964 after his death; Roche Dinkeloo & Associates completed the project. Dan Kiley designed the landscape. The hexagonal sanctuary and contrasting low roof and tall spire are defining elements.
https://visitcolumbusindiana.com/directory/the-lex-formerly-north-christian-church/
BCPL’s August 19, 2024 board minutes record successful removal of the cross from the spire. This establishes cross removal, not removal of the full spire.
https://static.libnet.info/frontend-images/pdfs/mybcpl/Board_Minutes/2024/8minutes.pdf
The current visitor-center listing uses The LEX and reports the property’s 2024 transfer to BCPL.
https://visitcolumbusindiana.com/directory/the-lex-formerly-north-christian-church/

briefs.name: Bartholomew County Courthouse
briefs.headline: The courthouse Columbus still walks into
facts: The Indiana Historical Bureau identifies Isaac Hodgson’s Second Empire courthouse as the county’s fourth, completed in 1874, with red brick and white limestone trim above a rusticated blue-limestone foundation.
https://secure.in.gov/history/state-historical-markers/find-a-marker/bartholomew-county-courthouse/

The same state marker records replacement of the original slate roof with standing-seam copper in 1953, major remodeling in 1968, interior restoration completed in 1998, and National Register listing in 1979.
https://secure.in.gov/history/state-historical-markers/find-a-marker/bartholomew-county-courthouse/

briefs.name: Cleo Rogers Memorial Library and Large Arch
briefs.headline: The plaza where brick meets bronze
facts: The library is I. M. Pei’s 1969 brick building. Its geometric massing relates to nearby First Christian; brick, concrete and limestone, with a coffered concrete ceiling, form the architectural vocabulary.
https://visitcolumbusindiana.com/directory/bartholomew-county-public-library/
Henry Moore’s Large Arch dates to 1971. The patinated-bronze sculpture on the plaza was a gift of J. Irwin and Xenia Miller. Its organic gateway contrasts with the surrounding rectilinear buildings.
https://visitcolumbusindiana.com/directory/large-arch/

briefs.name: Irwin Union Bank / Cummins Irwin Conference Center
briefs.headline: A bank designed to feel like a room in a garden
facts: Eero Saarinen designed the 1954 bank with landscape architect Dan Kiley. Its low glass-walled pavilion replaced the idea of a bank as a forbidding masonry institution with an open, visible interior.
https://visitcolumbusindiana.com/directory/cummins-inc-irwin-conference-center/

The visitor-center account describes Kevin Roche’s 1973 glass arcade and additions, and explains the later transition to Cummins conference and hospitality use. It identifies nine opaque ceiling domes as light shades, not skylights.
https://visitcolumbusindiana.com/directory/cummins-inc-irwin-conference-center/

briefs.name: Miller House and Garden
briefs.headline: One home, three designers, a complete world
facts: Newfields records the 1953 commission by J. Irwin and Xenia Simons Miller and credits Eero Saarinen, Alexander Girard and Dan Kiley. The design joins a flat-roofed stone-and-glass house, colorful textiles and geometric gardens.
https://discovernewfields.org/newfields/miller-house-and-garden

The visitor center dates the completed design to 1957. Newfields describes the honey-locust allée and confirms guided-tour-only access, with tours beginning at the visitor center rather than direct arrival at the house.
https://visitcolumbusindiana.com/directory/miller-house-and-garden/

briefs.name: Chaos I at The Commons
briefs.headline: The machine at the heart of The Commons
facts: The official local directory identifies Chaos I as Jean Tinguely’s steel-and-motor kinetic sculpture at The Commons, using wheels, gears and iron balls. It credits J. Irwin and Xenia Miller’s gift.
https://visitcolumbusindiana.com/directory/chaos-i/

There is a date conflict: the directory lists 1974; the visitor center’s public-art feature describes completion in 1975. Treat these as unresolved event dates until fabrication, installation and dedication records are checked.
